headline: A U.S. air travel meltdown, an auto-sector fight and a steadying oil market
summary: A network failure grounded U.S. departures on Friday and disrupted cross-border flights through the weekend. In Canada, the week turned on autos: Ottawa started a default clock on Stellantis over the Brampton plant sale, and Carney said a U.S. trade deal is closer but named Chinese automakers as a fallback. Oil eased despite continued Iranian attacks, and Nvidia's chief executive resigned in a China export scandal.

top.headline: Nationwide FAA ground stop cancels thousands of flights, including at Pearson
top.what: A network failure traced to a router in Arkansas halted U.S. departures for hours on Friday, with more than 9,000 cancellations that day and thousands more over the weekend; Air Canada cancelled about 250 flights. Flights are near normal by Monday, and a fight over a US$50-billion repair request is under way in Congress.
top.why: It was the most direct disruption of the week for GTA travellers and exposed how fragile cross-border air travel can be.

top.headline: Iran war: attacks on Bahrain and tankers continue while oil drifts lower
top.what: Iran claimed drone attacks on a U.S. radar in Bahrain and a string of tanker mine incidents, and a tanker was hit by a projectile leaving the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. Oil still fell about 2.5% on the week, with Brent near US$96, as forecasters see supply exceeding demand.
top.why: Oil prices feed straight into Ontario gasoline, heating and grocery costs, and into the Bank of Canada's rate decisions.

top.headline: Carney says a U.S. trade deal is closer, and names Chinese automakers as a fallback
top.what: Carney said talks with Washington are progressing but that he will not sign a deal that leaves Canada's auto sector unviable. On Sunday he said Canada could turn to Chinese, European or Japanese carmakers if the talks fail.
top.why: The outcome decides tariffs on Ontario-built vehicles and the future of tens of thousands of auto jobs.

top.headline: Ottawa starts 30-day default clock on Stellantis over Brampton plant sale
top.what: After Stellantis agreed to sell its idled Brampton assembly plant to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel, Ottawa formally put the company on notice under its subsidy agreement. The federal and Ontario governments are seeking a meeting with chief executive Antonio Filosa to try to stop or slow the sale.
top.why: The plant's fate affects thousands of Brampton-area auto workers and suppliers.

top.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigns amid China chip-export scandal
top.what: Nvidia's chief executive stepped down after reports tied the company's chip sales to a Singapore-based buyer linked to China, and the fallout reached Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The buyer, Megaspeed, said Sunday it has opened an internal probe; Nvidia reports results Tuesday.
top.why: Nvidia is one of the largest holdings in index funds and pension plans, so its turmoil moves Canadians' retirement savings.

top.headline: Midterm aftermath: Peltola nears Alaska win as Democrats prepare to take Congress
top.what: Democrat Mary Peltola leads Alaska's Senate race with about 49.9% of first-choice votes ahead of Wednesday's ranked-choice count, which would give Democrats 56 Senate seats. Democrats take control of both chambers in January.
top.why: A Democratic Congress changes the politics of U.S. tariffs on Canada, though it cannot override a presidential veto alone.

top.headline: Canada awaits October inflation, with forecasts of 3.0% to 3.3%
top.what: Economists expect Monday's Statistics Canada report to show inflation near September's 3.1%. It is the last reading before the Bank of Canada's Dec. 9 decision, where another rate hike is possible.
top.why: The number shapes mortgage and loan rates for Ontario households.

top.headline: Ukraine talks end without breakthrough as air attacks continue
top.what: U.S.-brokered talks ended without agreement, and Zelenskyy said American negotiators raised the idea of Ukraine leaving the Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, which Washington has not confirmed. Ukraine's arms donors meet in Brussels on Tuesday.
top.why: The war's course affects global energy and food prices and Canada's defence commitments.
